about: The Keplar security checklist, item by item, with status and evidence. Source of truth for docs/security-checklist.md (render: node scripts/security-checklist.mjs). Statuses: done (in code, evidence listed), policy (a written procedure the operator follows), accepted (dated risk acceptance in docs/security-policy.md), n/a (does not apply, with the reason), todo (fails CI).

sections.title: 1. Authentication and account security
sections.summary: Email links, passwords (scrypt), Google and Microsoft, TOTP, passkeys. Sessions are server-checked rows; sensitive changes need a recent sign-in.

items.item: Secure password hashing using Argon2id or an appropriate modern alternative
items.note: scrypt (Better Auth's hashPassword), an OWASP-listed alternative; Argon2id would add a native dependency to the serverless bundle.

items.item: Unique salts and properly configured hashing parameters
items.note: Random 16-byte salt per hash, scrypt N=16384, r=16, p=1, 64-byte key.

items.item: No plaintext passwords in databases, logs, or analytics

items.note: Enforced when KEPLAR_ADMIN_REQUIRE_MFA=1 is set in Vercel Production (fails closed). Turn it on after enrolling the admin authenticator; the variable is not set yet so the founder is not locked out.

items.item: MFA recovery with secure, limited-use recovery codes
items.note: 10 codes, hashed, each usable once; regenerating needs a current code.

items.item: Protection against MFA fatigue and repeated challenges
items.note: TOTP has no push prompts to fatigue; wrong codes are limited per IP, per session (the fifth ends the session) and per account, and the owner is emailed when codes are locked.
HMAC-SHA256 under a purpose-bound derived key; a reset token can never pass as a verification token.
30 minutes; single use through a fingerprint of the password hash current when issued.

items.item: Session invalidation after sensitive account changes
items.note: A password reset signs out every other device (sessions_valid_after); the secure link in notices signs out everywhere.
Per IP, IP+email and network+email limits; each trip is an auth.throttled security event, and three in ten minutes from one source email the owner.

items.item: Brute-force protection without easy account-lockout denial of service
items.note: Limits are keyed on the attacker (IP, network) with a high per-email ceiling instead of a hard lockout; email links and passkeys keep working for the real owner.
Identical answers and a dummy scrypt hash for unknown addresses (no timing tell).
Better Auth binds state to an encrypted cookie for Google/Microsoft; the MCP and connector flows store state per workspace and check it on callback.

items.item: OIDC nonce, issuer, audience, and signature validation
items.note: ID tokens are validated by Better Auth's provider implementations; Keplar additionally requires a provider-verified email claim.
Fixed callback URLs registered per provider; every post-login redirect goes through safeCallbackPath (same-origin paths only).
Sign-in linking only for Google and Microsoft with verified emails; connectors disconnect by deleting the sealed token.
Sign-in within 10 minutes for adding a passkey, enabling 2FA or new recovery codes, exporting data, creating API keys, immediate deletion; disabling 2FA needs a current code.

items.item: Secure logout that invalidates server-side sessions
items.note: Sign-out writes revoked_at; every request checks the row, so a revoked cookie stops working everywhere within 15 seconds.

items.item: No authentication secrets in browser storage when avoidable
items.note: HttpOnly cookies only. The one exception, the browser extension's scoped API key, is accepted risk AR-10.

sections.title: 2. Authorization and permissions
sections.summary: Every route checks the session and the workspace it acts on; the store scopes every query to a tenant; tests walk every route anonymously and as another user.

items.item: Server-side authorization on every protected operation

items.note: A new route that answers an anonymous caller fails the test until it is reviewed and listed with a reason.
Team roles (owner, member) decide billing, deletion and invitations; admin is a separate allow-list.

items.item: Attribute-based or policy-based access control where appropriate
items.note: Agent actions are decided by attributes of the action (risk, recipient known, links) and owner-set tool policy rows.
Public views redact hashes, tokens and internal fields (publicKey, publicSpec, export redaction).

items.item: Tenant isolation across every database query
items.note: Every collection operation takes the workspace id; cross-tenant reads exist only for system jobs on the system tenant.

items.item: Authorization checks in background jobs and queues
items.note: Jobs reload the workspace row and re-check plan, budget and kill switches before each slice.
Live collaboration streams need a signed room token bound to the user, room and role (viewer tokens are read-only).

items.item: Authorization checks for file downloads and exports
items.note: Exports need the account plus a recent sign-in; generated images are owner-only until used in a site; app files are keyed by app and environment.

items.item: Ownership checks before updates or deletions
Explicit authorization for impersonation or support access
items.note: No impersonation or log-in-as feature exists. Support works from the admin inbox; any look at content on request is written to the admin audit log (inventory section 9).

items.item: Separation of administrative and ordinary user capabilities
No reliance on hidden buttons or frontend route guards for security
Automated tests for cross-tenant access attempts

sections.title: 3. Session, cookie, and token protection
sections.summary: HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Lax, host-only cookies backed by server rows with idle and absolute expiry; HMAC tokens with purpose-bound keys; CSRF by Origin.

items.note: Lax: the app is a first-party site with OAuth returns.
Host-only cookies (no Domain attribute); business.keplar.one has its own session cookie and handoff.

items.item: Session ID rotation after login and privilege changes
items.note: Every sign-in mints a new session; a session waiting for its second factor is unusable until the code is given.
Session ids are server-minted on sign-in and never accepted from a URL or request body.
30 days unused (KEPLAR_SESSION_IDLE_DAYS); non-remembered sessions last one day.
180 days from sign-in regardless of activity (KEPLAR_SESSION_MAX_DAYS).
Browser sessions are server-checked cookies, not refresh tokens. Connector refresh tokens are provider-issued, stored sealed and exchanged server-side.
No refresh tokens are issued by Keplar (see above).
Disconnecting deletes the sealed token row; account deletion removes every connector.
Room tokens are HMAC-verified in constant time; Better Auth's session cache is an encrypted JWE.
One symmetric algorithm (HS256) is accepted; the header is not consulted to choose a key.
Tokens are bound to the room or purpose and the subject; a token for one purpose fails for another.
No asymmetric path exists, so an attacker cannot swap RS256 for HS256.
BETTER_AUTH_SECRET signs sessions, plan cookies, action links and seals connector tokens; rotation signs everyone out, so it is a documented procedure run on compromise, not a timer.
Sessions: revoked_at row; API keys: revokedAt looked up per request; action links: fingerprint changes on use; desktop codes: single use.

items.item: CSRF protection for cookie-authenticated state-changing requests
No session tokens in URL query strings
items.note: Sessions travel in cookies or the Authorization header only. Emailed links carry a one-time, short-lived token that the landing page only checks; the button's POST consumes it.

sections.title: 4. API and backend security
sections.summary: Parameterized SQL, validated and bounded bodies, SSRF-safe outbound fetches, per-route limits, signed webhooks, generic errors.

items.item: Output encoding for the destination context
items.note: React escapes app output; generated sites are re-escaped from decoded values by the sanitizer.

items.item: SQL injection prevention using parameterized queries

items.note: Postgres only; JSON document queries are parameterized SQL.
No shell receives user or model input: machine scripts are fixed strings; Studio code that spells destructive calls indirectly is detected and held.
No server-side template engine renders user input; prompts are string-built with fences and never evaluated.
A hand-written scanner that never resolves entities or DTDs; office documents are read as zipped XML with the same scanner.

items.item: Safe URL parsing and redirect validation

items.note: No CORS on cookie routes; wildcard only on the bearer-only public API, the public runtime scripts and the embed loader.
64 MB edge cap on every /api request, then per-route caps (JSON 5 MB, forms 24 KB, webhooks 256 KB).
Every list is bounded (20,000 rows max, 50 sessions, paged chats); no client-controlled unbounded scan.

items.item: API rate limiting by user, tenant, endpoint, and resource

items.note: One delayed retry for the database, bounded provider retries with backoff, Inngest step retries.
Routes copy named fields into typed patches; request bodies are never spread into a row.

items.item: Safe error handling without stack traces exposed to users
GraphQL depth and complexity limits, if applicable
items.note: No GraphQL endpoint.
Five-minute timestamp window and idempotency by webhook id; Stripe's SDK applies its own tolerance.

sections.title: 5. Frontend and browser security
sections.summary: A strict CSP with exact vendor origins, HSTS preload, framing denied, sanitizer and link guards for user content, no secrets or source maps in the bundle.

items.item: Nonce- or hash-based script restrictions where appropriate
items.note: AR-1: per-render inline flight data makes nonces force dynamic rendering; review Jan 2027.

items.item: Trusted Types where supported and useful
items.note: AR-2: three.js, CodeMirror and KaTeX use DOM sinks internally; compensated by escaping, the sanitizer and the generated-app innerHTML rule.

items.item: Safe HTML sanitization when rendering user-provided markup

items.note: dangerouslySetInnerHTML only for constants (JSON-LD, theme script); generated apps fail the no-unsafe-innerhtml check when markup is built from data.
No HTML rich-text editor: CodeMirror edits plain text and the CRDT carries text, rendered through the markdown renderer.
Vercel serves HTTPS only; CSP upgrade-insecure-requests; HSTS.
Runner messages are parsed against a strict shape from a frame Keplar created; generated apps hold no postMessage listeners by construction.

items.item: External links protected against unsafe opener access
Sensitive data excluded from browser caches
items.note: Every /api response is no-store; shared answer pages and account pages are dynamic and no-store.

items.item: No API secrets embedded in frontend bundles
items.note: NEXT_PUBLIC names are checked, and CI scans .next/static for credential patterns.
AR-3: vendor scripts are versionless; own scripts are same-origin content-hashed chunks.

items.item: Dependency security checks for frontend packages

sections.title: 6. Database and data protection
sections.summary: Neon Postgres over HTTPS, tenant-scoped rows, sealed secrets, scripted encrypted exports plus point-in-time restore, enforced retention and deletion.

items.note: Provider-managed (Neon); not independently verified, and the summary says so.

items.item: Database credentials stored in a secret manager
items.note: Vercel encrypted environment variables marked Sensitive.

items.item: Separate database roles for application, migrations, and administration
items.note: AR-5: backups use a separate read-only role; the app creates its own tables, so one app role today.
Tenant scoping is enforced by the store on every query; the document table carries RLS for the backup role boundary.
Isolation is tested against an in-process Postgres (pglite) and the file store.

items.item: Protection against cross-tenant joins and searches

items.note: AES-256-GCM with a scrypt-derived key when BACKUP_PASSPHRASE is set; the runbook requires it.
Off-site, passphrase kept apart from the file, never on Vercel or in git.
The restore path is tested against a fake database; the quarterly drill into a scratch Neon branch is an owner task whose date is recorded in the runbook (not yet held).
Neon point-in-time restore and branching.

items.item: Encryption key separation from encrypted data
items.note: Key material lives in Vercel's env; ciphertext lives in Neon; AAD binds each blob to its workspace and row.

items.item: Key management through a KMS or equivalent
items.note: AR-6: HKDF-derived keys from a Sensitive env secret instead of a KMS; review Jul 2027.

Rotation order and blast radius are written down (BETTER_AUTH_SECRET rotation signs everyone out and needs connector re-authorization); a software rotation would have to re-seal every token, which is scheduled with the KMS review (AR-6).
No raw IPs stored, cookie-free visit counts, content-free analytics, attachments never stored for Ask.

items.item: No production customer data in development environments without appropriate safeguards
items.note: Development uses the file store and dev tools; preview deployments have their own variables.
Schema changes are additive (CREATE IF NOT EXISTS); a Neon branch is taken before any risky change.
Export, secret-access and authorization-failure counts alert the owner past thresholds.

items.item: Prevention of accidental public database exposure
items.note: No public listener; credentials over TLS only; health reports booleans, never connection details.

sections.title: 7. File upload and storage security
sections.summary: Types decided by bytes, structural malware checks and an optional scanner, unguessable ids, sandboxed serving, no uploads in code paths.

items.item: Actual file content validation, not just extensions

items.note: Structural checks always; an external scanner when KEPLAR_MALWARE_SCAN_URL is set (fail-closed with KEPLAR_MALWARE_SCAN_REQUIRED).
Bytes live in Postgres per app and environment, never in a public bucket; served only through the app.
Files are served through the app by 120-bit random ids under a sandbox CSP; drafts use per-build tokens. Signed URLs are not needed while no object store is public.

items.item: Signed URL scope and expiration controls
items.note: See above; revisit when R2 is wired.
No listing endpoint; ids are unguessable.
SVG and any XML/HTML text are refused as uploads; generated SVG files are served sandboxed.

items.item: Isolation of user-generated HTML and active content

items.note: JPEG GPS data is stripped from imported product photos; uploads are served under a sandbox CSP with nosniff.

items.item: No executable uploads in application code directories
items.note: Uploads are data rows; app code files are model output limited to html, css, js, json and svg under APP_FILE.
Refused files are never stored; each refusal is an upload.rejected event and bursts alert the owner.

sections.title: 8. Cloud and infrastructure security
sections.summary: Serverless on Vercel with Neon; configuration is code and is tested; no containers or clusters of Keplar's own.

items.note: Per-purpose tokens, quarterly permission review.

items.item: Separate development, staging, and production environments
items.note: Vercel Production, Preview (noindex, own variables) and local development.
Serverless: no internal network exists; the database is reached only with a credential over TLS.
Vercel's platform layer plus strict host handling in the edge proxy.
No network of Keplar's own; sandboxes are isolated per job by the platform.
AR-7: no custom WAF rules on the current plan; Attack Challenge Mode is available during an attack.
Vercel-managed records; SPF, DKIM, DMARC for mail; CAA is a quarterly owner check.
No containers.
No containers.
No containers.
No containers; sandbox machines are platform-isolated microVMs.
Firecracker microVM isolation is the sandbox boundary (Vercel Sandbox).

items.item: No privileged containers without exceptional justification
items.note: No containers.

items.item: Workload identity instead of long-lived cloud credentials
items.note: AR-8: providers in use offer no OIDC federation for Vercel functions.

items.item: Kubernetes RBAC and admission policies if applicable
items.note: No Kubernetes.

items.item: Restriction of unnecessary outbound network traffic

items.note: A documented sequence (revoke tokens, delete sandboxes and snapshots, export and delete the database, remove DNS and the project) that a person runs; nothing is automated because teardown is rare and irreversible.
Keplar's own audit and security logs plus Vercel's and GitHub's activity logs.

sections.title: 9. Secrets and API key management
sections.summary: Everything in Vercel's encrypted env; scanned in source, CI and build output; sealed at rest; never logged, never prompted.

items.note: Yearly or on suspicion for provider and webhook secrets, on compromise for the auth secret; the calendar and the order of operations are written down. Providers offer no rotation API Keplar could drive safely.
The runbook lists every credential, where to rotate it and in which order (provider first, then Vercel, then redeploy).
Production, Preview and Development variable sets in Vercel.

items.item: Separate credentials per integration where feasible
Protection against secrets leaking into logs
Protection against secrets leaking into AI prompts
Protection against secrets leaking into crash reports
No secrets in public environment variables
Secure handling of OAuth refresh tokens

sections.title: 10. Payments and subscription security
sections.summary: Whop-hosted checkout for Keplar One plans and Stripe for Business sellers; signed, idempotent webhooks; server-side entitlements and atomic credits.

items.item: Payment provider-hosted checkout or other appropriately compliant payment flow
No unnecessary storage of card information

items.note: Card data never touches Keplar (hosted checkout and Stripe-hosted bank linking): SAQ A scope.
Each event is applied against the stored billing state; a late activation never resurrects a cancelled membership.

items.item: No trust in frontend subscription flags
items.note: The plan cookie is HMAC-signed, bound to the email and expires with the period; the database row is authoritative.

items.item: No trust in frontend-reported payment amounts
Price and plan IDs validated against server-side configuration

items.note: Per-IP and per-browser daily caps, deleted-login tombstones, verified email required for anything beyond Free.

items.item: Invoice and billing record access controls
items.note: The manage URL and billing status belong to the workspace; Whop hosts invoices behind the customer's own login.

items.item: Periodic reconciliation with the payment provider
items.note: On-demand sync against Whop plus the monthly review in the policy calendar.

sections.title: 11. AI and LLM security
sections.summary: Untrusted text fenced and sanitized; models never hold credentials; actions pass a deterministic firewall and approvals; budgets and step caps bound every run.

items.item: Clear separation of trusted instructions and untrusted content
Untrusted webpage content treated as data, not authority
items.note: Read pages inform answers only; any proposed action still passes the Firewall and approvals.

items.item: Untrusted repository instructions treated as data unless explicitly authorized
Prevention of system prompt and secret leakage
No API credentials exposed to models unless strictly necessary
items.note: Tokens are opened inside the request builder only; prompts never contain them.
No agent has filesystem or shell access on Keplar's servers.

items.item: Sensitive data redaction before model calls
Explicit controls for sending data to third-party models
Model provider retention and training policy review
Model output evaluation against malicious inputs

sections.title: 12. Autonomous agent security
sections.summary: Every action is tied to a workspace and a user, checked per tool, bounded by budgets, approved for anything that reaches the world, logged, and stoppable.

items.item: Every agent action tied to an authenticated user or authorized service identity
Explicit user authorization for the requested outcome
Separate permission checks for individual tools
No unrestricted access to the host operating system
Sandboxed code execution with resource limits
Isolated execution environments per user or task
Approval gates for purchases, payments, and transfers
items.note: No agent can pay: checkout is provider-hosted and user-driven; Business orders are placed by buyers on the seller's site.
Sites and apps go live only on the owner's explicit publish.

items.item: Approval gates for sending messages on a user's behalf

items.note: Keplar's own production changes come from merged pull requests and stamped deploys; no agent has deploy credentials.
Tool classes, auto-run flags and budgets are owner-edited rows with no tool API.

items.item: Prevention of duplicated side effects after retries
Idempotency for real-world actions where supported

items.note: A provider reply that is not a confirmed success is reported as an error.

items.item: Protection against agents modifying their own authorization policies
Prevention of agents bypassing approval gates
items.note: Approved edits are inspected again at execution; a blocked action never goes out.
No delegation API exists; each agent runs with the owner's rows and budgets.

items.item: Revocation of permissions during running tasks

sections.title: 13. GitHub and app-builder security
sections.summary: A ruleset on main, CI as the gate, CodeQL, dependency review, pinned actions, no secrets in CI, SBOM, stamped deploys.

items.item: GitHub App permissions restricted to necessary repositories
items.note: Keplar has no GitHub App; the GitHub connector is user OAuth with minimal scopes.
No GitHub App installation tokens.
Keplar receives no GitHub webhooks.
Ruleset on main: pull requests only, required CI check, no force pushes, no deletion.

items.item: Required code reviews for sensitive changes
items.note: CODEOWNERS names the sensitive paths; with one maintainer the review is the PR checklist plus CI, and code-owner review becomes required the day a second maintainer joins.
In-house probes of the running app (headers, anonymous and cross-user requests on every route); no commercial scanner.
No containers.
Registry and sha512 pinned for every package; third-party actions pinned to commits.
SHA-256 checksums for desktop releases; stamped web deployments. Code signing of installers is accepted risk AR-11.
CI holds no deploy credentials; Vercel's Git integration or the operator's stamped deploy ship code.

items.item: Protection against untrusted pull-request workflow execution
No privileged CI secrets available to untrusted code

sections.title: 14. Logging, monitoring, and incident response
sections.summary: Structured logs with request ids, a security event log with thresholds that email the owner, an audit log, retention, and a runbook with severities and drills.

items.note: Append-only rows under the system tenant with no delete route; Vercel logs are immutable on the platform; the runbook says never to delete during an incident.

items.item: Alerts for excessive failed authorization checks

items.note: Kill-switch and limit changes are config.change events; Vercel emails the team on environment changes.
Same procedure as above, exercised in the quarterly tabletop.
Who is told, when (72 hours, sooner if they must act), what the notice contains and that legal reviews it first; sending needs a person and a lawyer, not code.
A dated, blameless review in the findings log within a week, with a regression test and threat-model update; a people process by nature.
Quarterly tabletop; the runbook records the last date (none yet).

sections.title: 15. Privacy and compliance
sections.summary: A privacy policy written from the code, an inventory of data and processors, export and deletion in the product, consent-gated analytics.

items.item: Privacy policy matching actual data practices

items.note: Each processor's DPA is listed; accepting them in the provider dashboards and recording the date is an owner action.

items.item: International data transfer assessment where applicable
items.note: Processing is in the US under each processor DPA and SCCs; the privacy policy discloses it; an EU representative is an open legal decision.

items.item: Cookie disclosure and controls where required

items.note: 13+ terms, teen defaults and Family mode in code; purchases by minors remain a legal decision.
Export and deletion are self-serve in the product; other rights are handled by email with identity verified through a signed link to the account address, within 30 days.
Thresholds (72 hours to the authority, without undue delay to people at high risk), contents of the notice and legal review are written down; the decision is a human one.

items.item: Privacy impact assessments for high-risk processing
items.note: Required triggers and the assessment template are defined; each is a section in the feature design doc linked from the PR.

items.item: Restrictions on internal employee access to customer data
items.note: One operator today; access is through MFA-protected consoles and audited admin pages with no impersonation feature; the rule is written for the first hire.

items.item: Separation of customer content from product analytics
Contractual controls for AI providers and subprocessors
items.note: Provider terms and no-training settings are listed per processor; signing DPAs is an owner action recorded with a date in the inventory.

sections.title: 16. Business logic and abuse prevention
sections.summary: Server-side prices and limits, atomic counters, honeypots and verification against bots, cooldowns and takedowns for abusive workloads.

items.note: Keplar issues no coupons; promotions live in Whop, which validates them at its checkout.

items.item: Prevention of negative-price or negative-credit exploits
Protection against automated account creation abuse

items.note: Honeypots, MX checks and rate limits; no CAPTCHA by design (accessibility), which the policy records.

items.item: Prevention of unrestricted expensive API calls

items.note: Usage is metered server-side from provider responses; nothing client-reported is billed.
Concurrency caps, per-IP daily caps and new-device notices; a dedicated sharing detector is not built.

items.item: Automatic suspension of clearly abusive workloads with appropriate review

sections.title: 17. Security verification and governance
sections.summary: A threat model, a written lifecycle with gates and reviews, an accepted-risk register, disclosure with response targets, and evidence kept in the repository.

items.note: The PR template asks the security questions on every change and the policy requires a threat-model row before a new surface; a process, enforced by review rather than code.
Any change that crosses a trust boundary gets a design doc linked from the PR; with one maintainer this is a self-review against the threat model.

items.item: Fuzz testing for critical parsers and inputs

items.note: Yearly external test is an owner purchase in the policy calendar; none has been done, and /security says so.

items.item: Independent security review for high-risk releases
items.note: Yearly external review is budgeted in the policy calendar as an owner purchase; none has happened yet.

items.item: Vulnerability remediation deadlines based on severity

items.note: Quarterly restore drill into a scratch Neon branch and a yearly full rehearsal; dates are recorded in the backup runbook (none held yet).
Quarterly review of GitHub collaborators, Vercel team, admin emails, OAuth scopes and API keys, recorded in the findings log.
Quarterly inventory of every environment variable, rotation of anything older than a year, deletion of unused ones; recorded in the findings log.

sections.title: 18. Websites and apps Keplar generates
sections.summary: What every generated site and app gets automatically: the security and mobile checklist on each build (31 checks, deterministic repairs applied, the rest sent to the repair pass), plus the platform's own serving guarantees.

items.item: Security and mobile checklist runs on every build and is stored with the version
No inline, third-party or dynamic script; no inline handlers; no javascript: URLs; no frames, base or meta refresh
Every resource over HTTPS; new-tab links carry noopener; forms post to Keplar only; no password fields on static sites
No credentials in generated files; no HTML built from data with innerHTML; no remote module imports
Mobile viewport declared with zoom allowed; UTF-8 and language declared; every page titled
items.note: Repaired automatically when the model forgets.

items.item: Images scale to the screen, carry alt text, and load lazily below the first
items.note: Repaired automatically.

items.item: Layout adapts to width (media or container queries, clamp, minmax); no fixed page width; overflow fixed rather than hidden
items.note: Checked statically on every build and in a real browser at phone, tablet and desktop widths in the site QA run.

items.item: Readable text (12 px minimum) and 44 px tap targets

items.note: Repaired automatically.

items.item: Main landmark, one h1, labelled form fields
Served under a sandbox CSP with an opaque origin, nosniff, no framing by third parties, HSTS on custom domains
Forms and app APIs rate limited with honeypots; uploads scanned; app data isolated per app and environment
Drafts are noindex and token-protected; publishing is the owner's explicit action; abuse reports and takedown on every published page
Failed required checks block a quiet ship: they go to the model repair pass and into the build report
